title: SGM Network Study Dataset
text:
Preface
The purpose of this website is to document the data cleaning workflow for the SGM Network Study Dataset.
This website contains the full data cleaning process from start to finish. The completed dataset can be found in a secure Box folder only accessible to approved researchers at the Ecologies of Liberation Lab at University of Illinois.
As an ego network dataset, our data cleaning and scoring also contains uncommon workflows to score and prepare network data.
You can also find notes from the latest edits on GitHub.

text:
2.3 Creating Demographic Variables
Our survey asked participants to select all race/ethnicity, sexual identity, and religious affiliation categories that applied to them (i.e., check-all-that-apply items), while gender identity was a single-select item. This means the raw variables need to be collapsed into single, categorical variables before we can use them in analysis. Below we walk through that process for each of our four key demographic variables: race/ethnicity, gender identity, sexual orientation, and religious identity/affiliation.

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.4 Race and Ethnicity
Race and ethnicity was captured across 11 check-all-that-apply items (rei_1-rei_11), corresponding to White, Black, Asian, Pacific Islander, Native American, Native Hawaiian, MENA, Latine, Multiracial, Another racial identity, and Prefer not to answer, respectively. We’ll collapse these into a single race variable across four steps.

Step 1: Combine selections into a single string
First we recode missing values on each rei_* item to 0 (not selected), then paste together the labels of every category a participant selected into one string (race_combo). Respondents who selected nothing are labeled "None selected".


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    across(all_of(paste0("rei_", 1:11)), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), 0, .x)),

    race_combo = paste0(
      ifelse(rei_1 == 1, "White_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_2 == 1, "Black_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_3 == 1, "Asian_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_4 == 1, "Pacific Islander_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_5 == 1, "Native American_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_6 == 1, "Native Hawaiian_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_7 == 1, "MENA_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_8 == 1, "Latine_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_9 == 1, "Multiracial_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_10 == 1, "Another racial identity_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_11 == 1, "Prefer not to answer_", "")
    ),

    race_combo = case_when(
      race_combo == "" ~ "None selected",
      TRUE ~ str_remove(race_combo, "_$")
    )
  )




Step 2: Check the frequency of raw combinations
Before collapsing further, we look at how many unique combinations of race/ethnicity exist in the data and how common each one is. This tells us which combinations are common enough to deserve their own category, and which are rare enough to fold into a broader group.

Step 3: Collapse into final race/ethnicity categories
Using the frequencies above, we collapse race_combo into a smaller set of meaningful categories (race2):

Single-selection responses of White, Black, Asian, and Latine each become their own “Non-Latine” category (Latine becomes “Latine Non-White”); MENA stays on its own.
“White” + “Latine” is common enough on its own to warrant its own category (“White Latine”).
Every other multi-selection combination, along with single selections of smaller groups (Native American, Pacific Islander, Multiracial, Another racial identity), is combined into “Multiracial/ethnic”.
“Prefer not to answer” and blank responses are kept as their own categories.

We also set factor levels so tables and plots display in a consistent order.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    race2 = case_when(
      # Single-race categories
      race_combo == "Asian" ~ "Asian Non-Latine",
      race_combo == "Black" ~ "Black Non-Latine",
      race_combo == "Latine" ~ "Latine Non-White",
      race_combo == "White" ~ "White Non-Latine",
      race_combo == "MENA" ~ "MENA",

      race_combo == "White_Latine" ~ "White Latine",

      # All multiple selections go to Multiracial/ethnic

      race_combo == "Native American_Latine" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "White_Native American_Latine" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      # Single minority categories go to Multiracial/ethnic
      race_combo == "Native American" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Pacific Islander" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Another racial identity" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      # Complex combinations with Multiracial
      race_combo == "White_Asian_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "White_Black_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "White_Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "White_Black_Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "White_Native American_Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Black_Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Asian_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Multiracial_Another racial identity" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      # Everything selected
      race_combo == "White_Black_Asian_Pacific Islander_Native American_Native Hawaiian_MENA_Latine_Multiracial_Another racial identity" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      # Special cases
      race_combo == "Prefer not to answer" ~ "Prefer not to answer",
      race_combo == "Black_Prefer not to answer" ~ "Prefer not to answer",
      race_combo == "None selected" ~ "No response",

      TRUE ~ "Multiracial/ethnic"

    race2 = factor(

        "Latine Non-White",
        "White Non-Latine",
        "MENA",
        "White Latine",
        "Multiracial/ethnic",
        "Prefer not to answer",
        "No response"

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.5 Gender Identity
Gender identity (gi) was a single-select item, so no combining is needed here. We collapse the original response codes into three broader categories: cisgender men, cisgender women, and transgender/gender-diverse (tgd) individuals, combining response codes 5 through 10 (e.g., trans man, trans woman, nonbinary, genderqueer, etc.) into the tgd category due to small cell sizes.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(gender = case_when(
    is.na(gi) ~ NA,
    gi %in% c(1) ~ "cisman",
    gi %in% c(4) ~ "ciswoman",
    gi %in% c(5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) ~ "tgd",
    TRUE ~ NA
  ))

table(p2_data$gender, useNA = "ifany")

     305      356      216       77

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.6 Sexual Orientation
Sexual orientation was another check-all-that-apply item, with 10 identity options (si_1-si_10): Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Pansexual, Heterosexual/straight, Queer, Asexual, Demisexual, Questioning/unsure, and Another sexual identity. Because participants could select multiple identities that overlap in meaningful ways (e.g., someone selecting both “Queer” and “Bisexual” is likely using “Queer” as an umbrella term rather than a distinct identity), we build this variable up over several passes, with each pass collapsing the previous version a bit further.

Step 1: Combine selections into a single string
As with race/ethnicity, we first recode missing values to 0, then paste together every selected identity into a single string (sex_id_combo), which becomes our raw sex1 variable. We also count how many identities each person selected (selection_count), which we’ll use in later steps to decide how to collapse combinations.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    across(all_of(paste0("si_", 1:10)), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), 0, .x)),

    sex_id_combo = paste0(
      ifelse(si_1 == 1, "Gay_", ""),
      ifelse(si_2 == 1, "Lesbian_", ""),
      ifelse(si_3 == 1, "Bisexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_4 == 1, "Pansexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_5 == 1, "Heterosexual/straight_", ""),
      ifelse(si_6 == 1, "Queer_", ""),
      ifelse(si_7 == 1, "Asexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_8 == 1, "Demisexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_9 == 1, "Questioning/unsure_", ""),
      ifelse(si_10 == 1, "Another sexual identity_", "")
    ),

    sex_id_combo = case_when(
      sex_id_combo == "" ~ "None selected",
      TRUE ~ str_remove(sex_id_combo, "_$")
    ),

    selection_count = rowSums(
      cbind(si_1, si_2, si_3, si_4, si_5, si_6, si_7, si_8, si_9, si_10) == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    sex1 = sex_id_combo
  )

sex1_counts <- p2_data %>%
  count(sex1, sort = TRUE) %>%
  rename(frequency = n)

Step 2: Treat “Queer” and “Heterosexual/straight” as modifiers
Looking at the raw combinations above, two patterns stand out: people frequently pair “Queer” with a more specific identity (e.g., “Queer_Bisexual”), and some pair “Heterosexual/straight” with another identity (e.g., “Heterosexual/straight_Questioning/unsure”). In both cases the more specific identity is likely the better descriptor, so we recode these pairings to that other identity. The one exception is “Queer” + “Asexual”, which we keep coded as “Queer”.
Note that the two rules are not symmetric:

Queer is paired with all 8 other identities (Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Pansexual, Asexual, Demisexual, Questioning/unsure, Another sexual identity).
Heterosexual/straight is only explicitly paired with 5 (Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Pansexual, Questioning/unsure). Combinations of Heterosexual/straight with Asexual, Demisexual, Another sexual identity, or Queer are not covered by this recode.
For three-way combinations of Queer + Heterosexual/straight + one more identity, only + Bisexual and + Questioning/unsure are explicitly handled; other three-way combinations are not.

Any combination not covered by these rules simply falls through unchanged (kept as the raw sex_id_combo string). Single selections and “None selected” also pass through unchanged. This gives us sex2.

p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex2 = case_when(
      # Handle missing/none selected
      is.na(sex_id_combo) ~ NA_character_,
      sex_id_combo == "None selected" ~ "None selected",

      # Single selections - keep as is
      selection_count == 1 ~ sex_id_combo,

      # Rule 1: If combination includes "Queer" and one other identity, use the other identity
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Gay", sex_id_combo) ~ "Gay",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Lesbian", sex_id_combo) ~ "Lesbian",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Bisexual", sex_id_combo) ~ "Bisexual",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Pansexual", sex_id_combo) ~ "Pansexual",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Asexual", sex_id_combo) ~ "Queer", # Special case: Queer + Asexual = Queer
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Demisexual", sex_id_combo) ~ "Demisexual",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Questioning/unsure", sex_id_combo) ~ "Questioning/unsure",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Another sexual identity", sex_id_combo) ~ "Another sexual identity",

      # Rule 2: If combination includes "Heterosexual/straight" and one other identity, use the other identity
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Gay", sex_id_combo) ~ "Gay",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Lesbian", sex_id_combo) ~ "Lesbian",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Bisexual", sex_id_combo) ~ "Bisexual",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Pansexual", sex_id_combo) ~ "Pansexual",
      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Questioning/unsure", sex_id_combo) ~ "Questioning/unsure",

      # Rule 3: If both Queer AND Heterosexual/straight with one other, use the other identity
      selection_count == 3 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Bisexual", sex_id_combo) ~ "Bisexual",
      selection_count == 3 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Questioning/unsure", sex_id_combo) ~ "Questioning/unsure",

      # All other combinations remain as they are
      TRUE ~ sex_id_combo
    )
  )

Step 3: Simplify to single vs. multiple identities
For a simpler descriptive variable, we collapse everything that still contains multiple identities (indicated by an underscore in sex2) into a single “Multiple Sexual Identities” category, keeping single identities as they are. This gives us sex3.

    sex3 = case_when(
      is.na(sex2) ~ NA_character_,
      sex2 == "None selected" ~ "None selected",

      # Check if it's a single identity (no underscores in the cleaned version)
      !grepl("_", sex2) ~ sex2,

      # All multiple combinations get labeled as "Multiple Sexual Identities"
      TRUE ~ "Multiple Sexual Identities"
    ),

    # Convert to factor with logical ordering
    sex3 = factor(
      sex3,
      levels = c(
        "Gay", "Lesbian", "Bisexual", "Pansexual", "Heterosexual/straight",
        "Queer", "Asexual", "Demisexual", "Questioning/unsure",
        "Another sexual identity", "Multiple Sexual Identities", "None selected"

Step 4: Initial monosexual vs. plurisexual grouping
For our key sexual orientation variable, we group identities into monosexual (attraction to one gender: gay, lesbian, heterosexual/straight) versus plurisexual (attraction to multiple genders: bisexual, pansexual, demisexual), while keeping asexual, queer, questioning/unsure, and “another sexual identity” as their own distinct categories. Combinations that include a plurisexual identity (bisexual, pansexual, or demisexual) anywhere are coded as plurisexual. “Gay” + “Lesbian”, and monosexual + asexual combinations, are coded as monosexual. “Queer” + “Asexual” is coded as queer. Anything not covered by these rules is temporarily labeled “Other” so we can review it in the next step. This gives us sex4.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex4 = case_when(
      # Missing values
      is.na(sex2) ~ NA_character_,
      sex2 == "None selected" ~ "None selected",

      # Monosexual identities
      sex2 == "Gay" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Lesbian" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Heterosexual/straight" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Gay_Lesbian" ~ "Monosexual", # Gay+Lesbian combination
      sex2 == "Lesbian_Gay" ~ "Monosexual", # Gay+Lesbian combination

      # Monosexual + Asexual combinations
      sex2 == "Gay_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Asexual_Gay" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Lesbian_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Asexual_Lesbian" ~ "Monosexual",

      # Plurisexual identities
      sex2 == "Bisexual" ~ "Plurisexual",
      sex2 == "Pansexual" ~ "Plurisexual",
      sex2 == "Demisexual" ~ "Plurisexual",
      grepl("Bisexual", sex2) ~ "Plurisexual", # Any combination with Bisexual
      grepl("Pansexual", sex2) ~ "Plurisexual", # Any combination with Pansexual
      grepl("Demisexual", sex2) ~ "Plurisexual", # Any combination with Demisexual

      # Keep specific identities as is
      sex2 == "Asexual" ~ "Asexual",
      sex2 == "Queer" ~ "Queer",
      sex2 == "Questioning/unsure" ~ "Questioning/unsure",
      sex2 == "Another sexual identity" ~ "Another sexual identity",

      # Special case: Queer + Asexual = Queer
      sex2 == "Queer_Asexual" ~ "Queer",
      sex2 == "Asexual_Queer" ~ "Queer",

      # All other cases
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

Step 5: Final monosexual vs. plurisexual categorization
Reviewing the “Other” cases above, we found a few more combinations that clearly belong in the “Monosexual” category (e.g., “Gay” or “Lesbian” paired with “Questioning/unsure”, or “Gay”/“Lesbian” + “Queer” + “Asexual”). We add those rules here to produce our final variable, sex5. Anything still unaccounted for is kept as “Other” (rather than set to missing), since these are genuinely ambiguous combinations worth reviewing manually if needed.

    sex5 = case_when(
      # Keep all categories from sex4 except "Other"
      sex4 != "Other" ~ sex4,

      # Handle specific remaining combinations that should be categorized
      sex2 == "Gay_Queer_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Gay_Questioning/unsure" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Lesbian_Queer_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      grepl("^Gay_", sex2) & grepl("Questioning", sex2) ~ "Monosexual",
      grepl("^Lesbian_", sex2) & grepl("Questioning", sex2) ~ "Monosexual",

      # All remaining cases are coded as "Other" rather than NA
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),

    sex5 = factor(
      sex5,
      levels = c("Monosexual", "Plurisexual", "Asexual", "Queer",
                 "Questioning/unsure", "Another sexual identity", "Other", "None selected")
    )

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.7 Religious Identity
Religious affiliation was captured as check-all-that-apply items at two time points: current affiliation (rsi_curr_1-rsi_curr_26) and past affiliation (rsi_past_1-rsi_past_26). From these, we build a religious-trajectory variable, relid_life, classifying each respondent as Never, Former, or Current religious. This section mirrors the coding scheme used in a related analysis, Patterns of Religious Engagement, which uses this exact same raw dataset (sgm_ego_spss_DID_07_24_25.sav). Ambiguous or unclassifiable cases from that analysis were manually reviewed by two coders, and we reuse those resolved codes here rather than re-doing the review from scratch — because the row-based ID scheme lines up across both projects (both assign internal_id/ID as 1:nrow() on the full, unfiltered sample immediately after import), the manual codes can be joined back in directly.






Note



How is religious trajectory (relid_life) coded?

Classify affiliation per wave: Each respondent’s checked religious-affiliation items are collapsed to a single primary category for the past and current waves (rel_id2/rel_id1), using priority-ordered rules: non-religious/secular items first (Agnostic, Atheist, Non-religious, None, Secular Humanist), then Spiritual, then each denomination/tradition.
Group into broad categories: rel_id1/rel_id2 are grouped into rel_id (current) and rel_past_id (past). Only Buddhism, Daoism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Paganism, Sikhism, and Unitarian are grouped into Other; only Protestant, Orthodox, LDS, and Other Christian are grouped into Christian. Roman Catholic, Not Religious, and Spiritual keep their own labels. Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, and Zoroastrianism are not grouped — they pass through as their own raw labels, since the original scheme has no catch-all rule for them.
Classify trajectory: Comparing past vs. current group yields relid_life:

Never: not religious/spiritual in both waves
Former: religious (Christian/Roman Catholic/Other) in the past, not religious/spiritual now
Current: religious (Christian/Roman Catholic/Other) in both waves
Everything else is NA — this includes people who switched between traditions, people who became religious (not religious/spiritual in the past but religious now), and anyone whose past or current category is one of the five ungrouped raw labels above.

Manual review of ambiguous/NA cases: All NA respondents were independently reviewed by two coders across all religion responses (screen/RelID_Coding_062426.xlsx). Cases where both coders agreed on Current, Former, or Never were resolved; contradictions, missing data, or unresolved disagreements stayed NA. Resolved codes are merged back in by respondent ID and override the automatic classification only where a resolved code exists — everyone else keeps their automatic (possibly still-NA) classification.




Current Affiliation
We first collapse the 26 current-affiliation checkboxes into a single label per person (rel_id1). Non-religious/secular selections take priority — if a respondent checked any of Agnostic, Atheist, Non-religious, None, or Secular Humanist, they’re coded "Not Religious" regardless of what else they checked. We also keep the specific secular label on its own (not_rel) for reference. After Spiritual and the non-religious block, each remaining tradition is checked in turn.
We then group rel_id1 into a broader rel_id variable. As noted above, only 8 smaller/less-represented traditions get folded into "Other", and only 4 Christian sub-traditions get folded into "Christian" — Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, and Zoroastrianism are left as their own raw labels rather than grouped anywhere.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    not_rel = case_when(
      rsi_curr_1 == 1 ~ "Agnostic",
      rsi_curr_4 == 1 ~ "Atheist",
      rsi_curr_19 == 1 ~ "Non-religious",
      rsi_curr_20 == 1 ~ "None",
      rsi_curr_22 == 1 ~ "Secular Humanist"
    ),
    rel_id1 = case_when(
      rsi_curr_1 == 1 | rsi_curr_4 == 1 | rsi_curr_19 == 1 | rsi_curr_20 == 1 | rsi_curr_22 == 1 ~ "Not Religious",
      rsi_curr_24 == 1 ~ "Spiritual",
      rsi_curr_7  == 1 ~ "LDS",
      rsi_curr_8  == 1 ~ "Protestant",
      rsi_curr_9  == 1 ~ "Orthodox",
      rsi_curr_10 == 1 ~ "Roman Catholic",
      rsi_curr_11 == 1 ~ "Other Christian",
      rsi_curr_5  == 1 ~ "Bahai",
      rsi_curr_6  == 1 ~ "Buddhism",
      rsi_curr_12 == 1 ~ "Confucianism",
      rsi_curr_13 == 1 ~ "Daoism",
      rsi_curr_14 == 1 ~ "Hinduism",
      rsi_curr_15 == 1 ~ "Islam",
      rsi_curr_16 == 1 ~ "Jainism",
      rsi_curr_17 == 1 ~ "Judaism",
      rsi_curr_18 == 1 ~ "Native American",
      rsi_curr_21 == 1 ~ "Paganism",
      rsi_curr_23 == 1 ~ "Sikhism",
      rsi_curr_25 == 1 ~ "Unitarian",
      rsi_curr_26 == 1 ~ "Zoroastrianism"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rel_id = case_when(
      rel_id1 %in% c("Buddhism", "Daoism", "Hinduism", "Islam", "Judaism", "Paganism", "Sikhism", "Unitarian") ~ "Other",
      rel_id1 %in% c("Other Christian", "Protestant", "Orthodox", "LDS") ~ "Christian",
      TRUE ~ rel_id1
    )
  )

Past Affiliation
We repeat the exact same two-step process on the past-affiliation checkboxes (rsi_past_*), producing the raw per-tradition label rel_id2 and the grouped variable rel_past_id. The same grouping rule applies: only the same 8 traditions fold into "Other" and the same 4 Christian sub-traditions fold into "Christian"; Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, and Zoroastrianism again pass through ungrouped.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    rel_id2 = case_when(
      rsi_past_1 == 1 | rsi_past_4 == 1 | rsi_past_19 == 1 | rsi_past_20 == 1 | rsi_past_22 == 1 ~ "Not Religious",
      rsi_past_24 == 1 ~ "Spiritual",
      rsi_past_7  == 1 ~ "LDS",
      rsi_past_8  == 1 ~ "Protestant",
      rsi_past_9  == 1 ~ "Orthodox",
      rsi_past_10 == 1 ~ "Roman Catholic",
      rsi_past_11 == 1 ~ "Other Christian",
      rsi_past_5  == 1 ~ "Bahai",
      rsi_past_6  == 1 ~ "Buddhism",
      rsi_past_12 == 1 ~ "Confucianism",
      rsi_past_13 == 1 ~ "Daoism",
      rsi_past_14 == 1 ~ "Hinduism",
      rsi_past_15 == 1 ~ "Islam",
      rsi_past_16 == 1 ~ "Jainism",
      rsi_past_17 == 1 ~ "Judaism",
      rsi_past_18 == 1 ~ "Native American",
      rsi_past_21 == 1 ~ "Paganism",
      rsi_past_23 == 1 ~ "Sikhism",
      rsi_past_25 == 1 ~ "Unitarian",
      rsi_past_26 == 1 ~ "Zoroastrianism"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rel_past_id = case_when(
      rel_id2 %in% c("Buddhism", "Daoism", "Hinduism", "Islam", "Judaism", "Paganism", "Sikhism", "Unitarian") ~ "Other",
      rel_id2 %in% c("Other Christian", "Protestant", "Orthodox", "LDS") ~ "Christian",
      TRUE ~ rel_id2
    )
  )

           361            182             63            258              9 




Religious Trajectory (relid_life)
We compare rel_past_id to rel_id to classify each respondent’s trajectory. Only three combinations are explicitly handled — Never (not religious/spiritual at both waves), Former (religious at some point among Christian/Roman Catholic/Other, not religious/spiritual now), and Current (religious among Christian/Roman Catholic/Other at both waves). Everything else — including newly-religious respondents (not religious/spiritual in the past but religious now), anyone who switched between the grouped categories, and anyone whose past or current affiliation is one of the five ungrouped raw labels (Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, Zoroastrianism) — falls to NA, to be resolved by the manual coding step below.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    relid_life = case_when(
      # Never: not religious (or spiritual) in both waves
      rel_past_id %in% c("Not Religious", "Spiritual") &
        rel_id %in% c("Not Religious", "Spiritual") ~ "Never",

      # Former: religious in the past, not religious (or spiritual) now
      rel_past_id %in% c("Christian", "Roman Catholic", "Other") &
        rel_id %in% c("Not Religious", "Spiritual") ~ "Former",

      # Current: religious in the past AND still religious now
      rel_past_id %in% c("Christian", "Roman Catholic", "Other") &
        rel_id %in% c("Christian", "Roman Catholic", "Other") ~ "Current",

      # Everything else (e.g., switched traditions, became religious, or
      # involves an ungrouped raw label) → NA, resolved manually below
      TRUE ~ NA
    )
  )

table(p2_data$relid_life, useNA = "always")



Current  Former   Never    <NA> 
    311     366     170     107 


Click to see code
# Capture which respondents are NA under the automatic classification, before
# the manual codes get merged in below. We use this later purely to verify
# the merge did what we expect — it plays no role in the classification itself.
na_ids_auto <- p2_data$internal_id[is.na(p2_data$relid_life)]




Apply Manual Coding
Every respondent left NA above was independently reviewed by two coders (SK, NT) against their full set of religion responses, as part of the Patterns of Religious Engagement analysis. That review’s resolved codes live in the Final column of screen/RelID_Coding_062426.xlsx (copied into this project’s screen/ folder), keyed by respondent ID. Rows with a resolved Final value (Current, Former, or Never) override the automatic classification above; rows where the coders disagreed, lacked data, or otherwise couldn’t resolve the case are NA in Final and are left untouched — they keep whatever relid_life value they already had (which, since they all started out NA, means they simply remain NA).
The join key is internal_id, the sequential row number assigned to the full, unfiltered sample in 1_import.qmd. Because this section runs before any row filtering (the “Addressing Errors” step below hasn’t happened yet), and because internal_id was assigned immediately after import (mirroring how the ID was assigned in the Patterns of Religious Engagement project), the two ID schemes line up and the join is safe.

  left_join(manual_codes, by = c("internal_id" = "internal_id")) %>%
  mutate(relid_life = coalesce(Final, relid_life)) %>%

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.3 Creating Demographic Variables
Our survey asked participants to select all race/ethnicity, sexual identity, and religious affiliation categories that applied to them (i.e., check-all-that-apply items), while gender identity was a single-select item. This means the raw variables need to be collapsed into single, categorical variables before we can use them in analysis. Below we walk through that process for each of our four key demographic variables: race/ethnicity, gender identity, sexual orientation, and religious identity/affiliation.

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.4 Race and Ethnicity
Race and ethnicity was captured across 11 check-all-that-apply items (rei_1-rei_11), corresponding to White, Black, Asian, Pacific Islander, Native American, Native Hawaiian, MENA, Latine, Multiracial, Another racial identity, and Prefer not to answer, respectively. We’ll collapse these into a single race variable across four steps.

Step 1: Combine selections into a single string
First we recode missing values on each rei_* item to 0 (not selected), then paste together the labels of every category a participant selected into one string (race_combo). Respondents who selected nothing are labeled "None selected".


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    across(all_of(paste0("rei_", 1:11)), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), 0, .x)),

    race_combo = paste0(
      ifelse(rei_1 == 1, "White_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_2 == 1, "Black_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_3 == 1, "Asian_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_4 == 1, "Pacific Islander_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_5 == 1, "Native American_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_6 == 1, "Native Hawaiian_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_7 == 1, "MENA_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_8 == 1, "Latine_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_9 == 1, "Multiracial_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_10 == 1, "Another racial identity_", ""),
      ifelse(rei_11 == 1, "Prefer not to answer_", "")
    ),

    race_combo = case_when(
      race_combo == "" ~ "None selected",
      TRUE ~ str_remove(race_combo, "_$")
    )
  )




Step 2: Check the frequency of raw combinations
Before collapsing further, we look at how many unique combinations of race/ethnicity exist in the data and how common each one is. This tells us which combinations are common enough to deserve their own category, and which are rare enough to fold into a broader group.

Step 3: Collapse into final race/ethnicity categories

We also set factor levels so tables and plots display in a consistent order.

      # Single minority categories go to Multiracial/ethnic
      race_combo == "Native American" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Pacific Islander" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Another racial identity" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      # Complex combinations with Multiracial
      race_combo == "White_Asian_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "White_Black_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "White_Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      race_combo == "White_Native American_Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Black_Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Latine_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Asian_Multiracial" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",
      race_combo == "Multiracial_Another racial identity" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      # Everything selected
      race_combo == "White_Black_Asian_Pacific Islander_Native American_Native Hawaiian_MENA_Latine_Multiracial_Another racial identity" ~ "Multiracial/ethnic",

      # Special cases
      race_combo == "Prefer not to answer" ~ "Prefer not to answer",
      race_combo == "Black_Prefer not to answer" ~ "Prefer not to answer",
      race_combo == "None selected" ~ "No response",

        "Latine Non-White",
        "White Non-Latine",
        "MENA",
        "White Latine",
        "Multiracial/ethnic",
        "Prefer not to answer",
        "No response"

2.5 Gender Identity
Gender identity (gi) was a single-select item, so no combining is needed here. We collapse the original response codes into three broader categories: cisgender men, cisgender women, and transgender/gender-diverse (tgd) individuals, combining response codes 5 through 10 (e.g., trans man, trans woman, nonbinary, genderqueer, etc.) into the tgd category due to small cell sizes.

  mutate(gender = case_when(
    is.na(gi) ~ NA,
    gi %in% c(1) ~ "cisman",
    gi %in% c(4) ~ "ciswoman",
    gi %in% c(5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) ~ "tgd",
    TRUE ~ NA

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.6 Sexual Orientation
Sexual orientation was another check-all-that-apply item, with 10 identity options (si_1-si_10): Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Pansexual, Heterosexual/straight, Queer, Asexual, Demisexual, Questioning/unsure, and Another sexual identity. Because participants could select multiple identities that overlap in meaningful ways (e.g., someone selecting both “Queer” and “Bisexual” is likely using “Queer” as an umbrella term rather than a distinct identity), we build this variable up over several passes, with each pass collapsing the previous version a bit further.

Step 1: Combine selections into a single string
As with race/ethnicity, we first recode missing values to 0, then paste together every selected identity into a single string (sex_id_combo), which becomes our raw sex1 variable. We also count how many identities each person selected (selection_count), which we’ll use in later steps to decide how to collapse combinations.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    across(all_of(paste0("si_", 1:10)), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), 0, .x)),

    sex_id_combo = paste0(
      ifelse(si_1 == 1, "Gay_", ""),
      ifelse(si_2 == 1, "Lesbian_", ""),
      ifelse(si_3 == 1, "Bisexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_4 == 1, "Pansexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_5 == 1, "Heterosexual/straight_", ""),
      ifelse(si_6 == 1, "Queer_", ""),
      ifelse(si_7 == 1, "Asexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_8 == 1, "Demisexual_", ""),
      ifelse(si_9 == 1, "Questioning/unsure_", ""),
      ifelse(si_10 == 1, "Another sexual identity_", "")
    ),

    sex_id_combo = case_when(
      sex_id_combo == "" ~ "None selected",
      TRUE ~ str_remove(sex_id_combo, "_$")
    ),

    selection_count = rowSums(
      cbind(si_1, si_2, si_3, si_4, si_5, si_6, si_7, si_8, si_9, si_10) == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    sex1 = sex_id_combo
  )

Step 2: Treat “Queer” and “Heterosexual/straight” as modifiers
Looking at the raw combinations above, two patterns stand out: people frequently pair “Queer” with a more specific identity (e.g., “Queer_Bisexual”), and some pair “Heterosexual/straight” with another identity (e.g., “Heterosexual/straight_Questioning/unsure”). In both cases the more specific identity is likely the better descriptor, so we recode these pairings to that other identity. The one exception is “Queer” + “Asexual”, which we keep coded as “Queer”.
Note that the two rules are not symmetric:

Queer is paired with all 8 other identities (Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Pansexual, Asexual, Demisexual, Questioning/unsure, Another sexual identity).
Heterosexual/straight is only explicitly paired with 5 (Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Pansexual, Questioning/unsure). Combinations of Heterosexual/straight with Asexual, Demisexual, Another sexual identity, or Queer are not covered by this recode.
For three-way combinations of Queer + Heterosexual/straight + one more identity, only + Bisexual and + Questioning/unsure are explicitly handled; other three-way combinations are not.

Any combination not covered by these rules simply falls through unchanged (kept as the raw sex_id_combo string). Single selections and “None selected” also pass through unchanged. This gives us sex2.

      # Single selections - keep as is
      selection_count == 1 ~ sex_id_combo,

      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Queer", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Another sexual identity", sex_id_combo) ~ "Another sexual identity",

      # Rule 2: If combination includes "Heterosexual/straight" and one other identity, use the other identity

      selection_count == 2 & grepl("Heterosexual/straight", sex_id_combo) & grepl("Lesbian", sex_id_combo) ~ "Lesbian",

Step 3: Simplify to single vs. multiple identities
For a simpler descriptive variable, we collapse everything that still contains multiple identities (indicated by an underscore in sex2) into a single “Multiple Sexual Identities” category, keeping single identities as they are. This gives us sex3.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex3 = case_when(
      is.na(sex2) ~ NA_character_,
      sex2 == "None selected" ~ "None selected",

      # Check if it's a single identity (no underscores in the cleaned version)
      !grepl("_", sex2) ~ sex2,

      # All multiple combinations get labeled as "Multiple Sexual Identities"
      TRUE ~ "Multiple Sexual Identities"
    ),

    # Convert to factor with logical ordering
    sex3 = factor(
      sex3,
      levels = c(
        "Gay", "Lesbian", "Bisexual", "Pansexual", "Heterosexual/straight",
        "Queer", "Asexual", "Demisexual", "Questioning/unsure",
        "Another sexual identity", "Multiple Sexual Identities", "None selected"
      )
    )
  )

sex3_counts <- p2_data %>%
  count(sex3, sort = TRUE) %>%
  rename(frequency = n)

10 Demisexual                         1




Step 4: Initial monosexual vs. plurisexual grouping
For our key sexual orientation variable, we group identities into monosexual (attraction to one gender: gay, lesbian, heterosexual/straight) versus plurisexual (attraction to multiple genders: bisexual, pansexual, demisexual), while keeping asexual, queer, questioning/unsure, and “another sexual identity” as their own distinct categories. Combinations that include a plurisexual identity (bisexual, pansexual, or demisexual) anywhere are coded as plurisexual. “Gay” + “Lesbian”, and monosexual + asexual combinations, are coded as monosexual. “Queer” + “Asexual” is coded as queer. Anything not covered by these rules is temporarily labeled “Other” so we can review it in the next step. This gives us sex4.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex4 = case_when(
      # Missing values
      is.na(sex2) ~ NA_character_,
      sex2 == "None selected" ~ "None selected",

      # Monosexual identities
      sex2 == "Gay" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Lesbian" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Heterosexual/straight" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Gay_Lesbian" ~ "Monosexual", # Gay+Lesbian combination
      sex2 == "Lesbian_Gay" ~ "Monosexual", # Gay+Lesbian combination

      # Monosexual + Asexual combinations
      sex2 == "Gay_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Asexual_Gay" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Lesbian_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Asexual_Lesbian" ~ "Monosexual",

      # Plurisexual identities
      sex2 == "Bisexual" ~ "Plurisexual",
      sex2 == "Pansexual" ~ "Plurisexual",
      sex2 == "Demisexual" ~ "Plurisexual",
      grepl("Bisexual", sex2) ~ "Plurisexual", # Any combination with Bisexual
      grepl("Pansexual", sex2) ~ "Plurisexual", # Any combination with Pansexual
      grepl("Demisexual", sex2) ~ "Plurisexual", # Any combination with Demisexual

      # Keep specific identities as is
      sex2 == "Asexual" ~ "Asexual",
      sex2 == "Queer" ~ "Queer",
      sex2 == "Questioning/unsure" ~ "Questioning/unsure",
      sex2 == "Another sexual identity" ~ "Another sexual identity",

      # Special case: Queer + Asexual = Queer
      sex2 == "Queer_Asexual" ~ "Queer",
      sex2 == "Asexual_Queer" ~ "Queer",

      # All other cases
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

sex4_counts <- p2_data %>%
  count(sex4, sort = TRUE) %>%
  rename(frequency = n)

Step 5: Final monosexual vs. plurisexual categorization
Reviewing the “Other” cases above, we found a few more combinations that clearly belong in the “Monosexual” category (e.g., “Gay” or “Lesbian” paired with “Questioning/unsure”, or “Gay”/“Lesbian” + “Queer” + “Asexual”). We add those rules here to produce our final variable, sex5. Anything still unaccounted for is kept as “Other” (rather than set to missing), since these are genuinely ambiguous combinations worth reviewing manually if needed.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex5 = case_when(
      # Keep all categories from sex4 except "Other"
      sex4 != "Other" ~ sex4,

      # Handle specific remaining combinations that should be categorized
      sex2 == "Gay_Queer_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Gay_Questioning/unsure" ~ "Monosexual",
      sex2 == "Lesbian_Queer_Asexual" ~ "Monosexual",
      grepl("^Gay_", sex2) & grepl("Questioning", sex2) ~ "Monosexual",
      grepl("^Lesbian_", sex2) & grepl("Questioning", sex2) ~ "Monosexual",

      # All remaining cases are coded as "Other" rather than NA
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),

    # Convert to factor with logical ordering
    sex5 = factor(
      sex5,
      levels = c("Monosexual", "Plurisexual", "Asexual", "Queer",
                 "Questioning/unsure", "Another sexual identity", "Other", "None selected")
    )
  )

title: 2  Demographic Variables
text:
2.7 Religious Identity
Religious affiliation was captured as check-all-that-apply items at two time points: current affiliation (rsi_curr_1-rsi_curr_26) and past affiliation (rsi_past_1-rsi_past_26). From these, we build a religious-trajectory variable, relid_life, classifying each respondent as Never, Former, or Current religious. This section mirrors the coding scheme used in a related analysis, Patterns of Religious Engagement, which uses this exact same raw dataset (sgm_ego_spss_DID_07_24_25.sav). Ambiguous or unclassifiable cases from that analysis were manually reviewed by two coders, and we reuse those resolved codes here rather than re-doing the review from scratch — because the row-based ID scheme lines up across both projects (both assign internal_id/ID as 1:nrow() on the full, unfiltered sample immediately after import), the manual codes can be joined back in directly.






Note



How is religious trajectory (relid_life) coded?

Classify affiliation per wave: Each respondent’s checked religious-affiliation items are collapsed to a single primary category for the past and current waves (rel_past_id2/rel_curr_id1), using priority-ordered rules: non-religious/secular items first (Agnostic, Atheist, Non-religious, None, Secular Humanist), then Spiritual, then each denomination/tradition.
Group into broad categories: rel_curr_id1/rel_past_id2 are grouped into rel_curr_id (current) and rel_past_id (past). Only Buddhism, Daoism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Paganism, Sikhism, and Unitarian are grouped into Other; only Protestant, Orthodox, LDS, and Other Christian are grouped into Christian. Roman Catholic, Not Religious, and Spiritual keep their own labels. Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, and Zoroastrianism are not grouped — they pass through as their own raw labels, since the original scheme has no catch-all rule for them.
Classify trajectory: Comparing past vs. current group yields relid_life:

Never: not religious/spiritual in both waves
Former: religious (Christian/Roman Catholic/Other) in the past, not religious/spiritual now
Current: religious (Christian/Roman Catholic/Other) in both waves
Everything else is NA — this includes people who switched between traditions, people who became religious (not religious/spiritual in the past but religious now), and anyone whose past or current category is one of the five ungrouped raw labels above.

Manual review of ambiguous/NA cases: All NA respondents were independently reviewed by two coders across all religion responses (screen/RelID_Coding_062426.xlsx). Cases where both coders agreed on Current, Former, or Never were resolved; contradictions, missing data, or unresolved disagreements stayed NA. Resolved codes are merged back in by respondent ID and override the automatic classification only where a resolved code exists — everyone else keeps their automatic (possibly still-NA) classification.




Current Affiliation
We first collapse the 26 current-affiliation checkboxes into a single label per person (rel_curr_id1). Non-religious/secular selections take priority — if a respondent checked any of Agnostic, Atheist, Non-religious, None, or Secular Humanist, they’re coded "Not Religious" regardless of what else they checked. We also keep the specific secular label on its own (not_rel) for reference. After Spiritual and the non-religious block, each remaining tradition is checked in turn.
We then group rel_curr_id1 into a broader rel_curr_id variable. As noted above, only 8 smaller/less-represented traditions get folded into "Other", and only 4 Christian sub-traditions get folded into "Christian" — Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, and Zoroastrianism are left as their own raw labels rather than grouped anywhere.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    not_rel = case_when(
      rsi_curr_1 == 1 ~ "Agnostic",
      rsi_curr_4 == 1 ~ "Atheist",
      rsi_curr_19 == 1 ~ "Non-religious",
      rsi_curr_20 == 1 ~ "None",
      rsi_curr_22 == 1 ~ "Secular Humanist"
    ),
    rel_curr_id1 = case_when(
      rsi_curr_1 == 1 | rsi_curr_4 == 1 | rsi_curr_19 == 1 | rsi_curr_20 == 1 | rsi_curr_22 == 1 ~ "Not Religious",
      rsi_curr_24 == 1 ~ "Spiritual",
      rsi_curr_7  == 1 ~ "LDS",
      rsi_curr_8  == 1 ~ "Protestant",
      rsi_curr_9  == 1 ~ "Orthodox",
      rsi_curr_10 == 1 ~ "Roman Catholic",
      rsi_curr_11 == 1 ~ "Other Christian",
      rsi_curr_5  == 1 ~ "Bahai",
      rsi_curr_6  == 1 ~ "Buddhism",
      rsi_curr_12 == 1 ~ "Confucianism",
      rsi_curr_13 == 1 ~ "Daoism",
      rsi_curr_14 == 1 ~ "Hinduism",
      rsi_curr_15 == 1 ~ "Islam",
      rsi_curr_16 == 1 ~ "Jainism",
      rsi_curr_17 == 1 ~ "Judaism",
      rsi_curr_18 == 1 ~ "Native American",
      rsi_curr_21 == 1 ~ "Paganism",
      rsi_curr_23 == 1 ~ "Sikhism",
      rsi_curr_25 == 1 ~ "Unitarian",
      rsi_curr_26 == 1 ~ "Zoroastrianism"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rel_curr_id = case_when(
      rel_curr_id1 %in% c("Buddhism", "Daoism", "Hinduism", "Islam", "Judaism", "Paganism", "Sikhism", "Unitarian") ~ "Other",
      rel_curr_id1 %in% c("Other Christian", "Protestant", "Orthodox", "LDS") ~ "Christian",
      TRUE ~ rel_curr_id1
    )
  )

           159            499             54            115             49 




Past Affiliation
We repeat the exact same two-step process on the past-affiliation checkboxes (rsi_past_*), producing the raw per-tradition label rel_past_id2 and the grouped variable rel_past_id. The same grouping rule applies: only the same 8 traditions fold into "Other" and the same 4 Christian sub-traditions fold into "Christian"; Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, and Zoroastrianism again pass through ungrouped.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    rel_past_id2 = case_when(
      rsi_past_1 == 1 | rsi_past_4 == 1 | rsi_past_19 == 1 | rsi_past_20 == 1 | rsi_past_22 == 1 ~ "Not Religious",
      rsi_past_24 == 1 ~ "Spiritual",
      rsi_past_7  == 1 ~ "LDS",
      rsi_past_8  == 1 ~ "Protestant",
      rsi_past_9  == 1 ~ "Orthodox",
      rsi_past_10 == 1 ~ "Roman Catholic",
      rsi_past_11 == 1 ~ "Other Christian",
      rsi_past_5  == 1 ~ "Bahai",
      rsi_past_6  == 1 ~ "Buddhism",
      rsi_past_12 == 1 ~ "Confucianism",
      rsi_past_13 == 1 ~ "Daoism",
      rsi_past_14 == 1 ~ "Hinduism",
      rsi_past_15 == 1 ~ "Islam",
      rsi_past_16 == 1 ~ "Jainism",
      rsi_past_17 == 1 ~ "Judaism",
      rsi_past_18 == 1 ~ "Native American",
      rsi_past_21 == 1 ~ "Paganism",
      rsi_past_23 == 1 ~ "Sikhism",
      rsi_past_25 == 1 ~ "Unitarian",
      rsi_past_26 == 1 ~ "Zoroastrianism"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rel_past_id = case_when(
      rel_past_id2 %in% c("Buddhism", "Daoism", "Hinduism", "Islam", "Judaism", "Paganism", "Sikhism", "Unitarian") ~ "Other",
      rel_past_id2 %in% c("Other Christian", "Protestant", "Orthodox", "LDS") ~ "Christian",
      TRUE ~ rel_past_id2
    )
  )

table(p2_data$rel_past_id)



     Christian  Not Religious          Other Roman Catholic      Spiritual 
           361            182             63            258              9 




Religious Trajectory (relid_life)
We compare rel_past_id to rel_curr_id to classify each respondent’s trajectory. Only three combinations are explicitly handled — Never (not religious/spiritual at both waves), Former (religious at some point among Christian/Roman Catholic/Other, not religious/spiritual now), and Current (religious among Christian/Roman Catholic/Other at both waves). Everything else — including newly-religious respondents (not religious/spiritual in the past but religious now), anyone who switched between the grouped categories, and anyone whose past or current affiliation is one of the five ungrouped raw labels (Bahai, Confucianism, Jainism, Native American, Zoroastrianism) — falls to NA, to be resolved by the manual coding step below.


Click to see code
p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  mutate(
    relid_life = case_when(
      # Never: not religious (or spiritual) in both waves
      rel_past_id %in% c("Not Religious", "Spiritual") &
        rel_curr_id %in% c("Not Religious", "Spiritual") ~ "Never",

      # Former: religious in the past, not religious (or spiritual) now
      rel_past_id %in% c("Christian", "Roman Catholic", "Other") &
        rel_curr_id %in% c("Not Religious", "Spiritual") ~ "Former",

      # Current: religious in the past AND still religious now
      rel_past_id %in% c("Christian", "Roman Catholic", "Other") &
        rel_curr_id %in% c("Christian", "Roman Catholic", "Other") ~ "Current",

      # Everything else (e.g., switched traditions, became religious, or
      # involves an ungrouped raw label) → NA, resolved manually below
      TRUE ~ NA
    )
  )

table(p2_data$relid_life, useNA = "always")



Current  Former   Never    <NA> 
    311     366     170     107 


Click to see code
# Capture which respondents are NA under the automatic classification, before
# the manual codes get merged in below. We use this later purely to verify
# the merge did what we expect — it plays no role in the classification itself.
na_ids_auto <- p2_data$internal_id[is.na(p2_data$relid_life)]




Manual Coding
Because we knew our algorithm would not be 100% effective, every respondent left NA above was independently reviewed by two coders (SK, NT) against their full set of religion responses, as part of the Patterns of Religious Engagement analysis. That review’s resolved codes live in the Final column of screen/RelID_Coding_062426.xlsx (copied into this project’s screen/ folder), keyed by respondent ID. Rows with a resolved Final value (Current, Former, or Never) override the automatic classification above; rows where the coders disagreed, lacked data, or otherwise couldn’t resolve the case are NA in Final and are left untouched — they keep whatever relid_life value they already had (which, since they all started out NA, means they simply remain NA).


Apply Manual Coding
The join key is internal_id, the sequential row number assigned to the full, unfiltered sample in 1_import.qmd. Because this section runs before any row filtering (the “Addressing Errors” step below hasn’t happened yet), and because internal_id was assigned immediately after import (mirroring how the ID was assigned in the Patterns of Religious Engagement project), the two ID schemes line up and the join is safe.


Click to see code
rel_curr_id_code <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(here("screen", "RelID_Coding_062426.xlsx"))

manual_codes <- rel_curr_id_code %>%
  filter(!is.na(Final)) %>%
  select(internal_id, Final)

p2_data <- p2_data %>%
  left_join(manual_codes, by = c("internal_id" = "internal_id")) %>%
  mutate(relid_life = coalesce(Final, relid_life)) %>%
  select(-Final)

table(p2_data$relid_life, useNA = "always")



Current  Former   Never    <NA> 
    326     363     173      92 




Export Cleaned ResponseID + Religious Identity


Click to see code
relid_data <- p2_data %>%
  select(responseid, rel_curr_id, rel_past_id, relid_life)

openxlsx::write.xlsx(relid_data, here("external_files/relid_codes_072126.xlsx"))

How does it work?

This data cleaning workflow is performed locally on a laptop.
Each phase is separated by its own R script file (.qmd file)
Thus, each R script chapter reflects the actual underlying code used to clean and process data.


This means that you can also directly suggest edits or corrections online (see section below) which will be reflected in the data cleaning workflow.


Everytime the R code is changed or updated, GitHub will track and contain a comment (user must provide) that denotes what changes were made.

3  Ego-Alter Variables
text:
3.4 Correct Errors Variable Names

Alter Service Attendance
It looks like two variables were named incorrectly. The variable to measure service attendance of an alter is typically alt_ra_X where X = the number of the alter. Here’s what that variable label looks like:

get_variable_labels(p3_data$alt_ra_1)

[1] "To the best of your knowledge, aside from weddings and funerals, how often does [QID1089-ChoiceTextEntryValue-1] attend religious services?"


However, there are two variables with incorrect variable names.

get_variable_labels(p3_data$alr_ra_2)

[1] "To the best of your knowledge, aside from weddings and funerals, how often does [QID1089-ChoiceTextEntryValue-2] attend religious services?"

get_variable_labels(p3_data$alr_ra_3)

[1] "To the best of your knowledge, aside from weddings and funerals, how often does [QID1089-ChoiceTextEntryValue-3] attend religious services?"


Here, it’s clear that the variables measure the same construct, yet they are named incorrectly. Let’s fix that.

p3_data <- rename(p3_data,
                    alt_ra_2 = alr_ra_2,
                    alt_ra_3 = alr_ra_3)

title: 3  Ego-Alter Variables
text:
3.5 Recode Values

Alter-Alter Ties
The value labels are coded in a manner that will bias our analyses later.

get_variable_labels(p3_data$ap1_2)

[1] "Do [QID1089-ChoiceTextEntryValue-1] and [QID1089-ChoiceTextEntryValue-2] talk to each other independently of you? In other words, do they have a relationship independently of you? For example, your parent and sibling might talk, but your parent and coworker might not."

get_value_labels(p3_data$ap1_2)

                  Yes                    No          I don't know 
                    1                     2                     3 
Choose Not to Respond 
                    4 


As you can see, No = 2 while Yes = 1. However, when we calculate the sum, we want to make sure that we only count the Yes’s, thus it makes more sense to code No as 0, and Yes as 1.

p3_data <- p3_data |>
  mutate(across(contains("ap1_") | contains("ap2_") | contains("ap3_") | contains("ap4_") | contains("ap5_") | contains("ap6_") | contains("ap7_") | contains("ap8_") | contains("ap9_"), ~ifelse(. == 2, 0, .)))

The code above specifies: If value is equal to 2, then code as 0. If the condition is not true, leave as is.


Religious Importance

get_variable_labels(p3_data$alt_ri_1)

3.5 Create Ego Network Data
Let’s create our ego network data!

ego_object <- onefile_to_egor(
  egos = p3_data,
  ID.vars = list(ego = "egoid"),
  attr.start.col = "alt_rel_1", # Name of Variable with the first alter attribute
  attr.end.col = "alt_smv_conc_10", # Name of variable with last alter attribute
  max.alters = 10, # Number of maximum alters that were named by participants
  aa.first.var = "ap1_2") # Name of first alter-alter variable


saveRDS(ego_object, here("work_data/egor_object.Rds"))

The resulting output is an object that is comprised of 3 different datasets: EGO data (N = 953, Variables = 548), Alter data (N = 9,530, Variables = 145), and Alter-Alter Tie Data (N = 14,460; Variabels = 4).

Create Merged Dataset
Having created the three different datasets, we want to create a dataset that merges the ego and alter data.

p3.1_data <- ego_object$ego

p3.2_data <- ego_object$alter

What we’ve done above is create two datasets based on ego and alter (respectively). Now using the .egoID variable, lets merge these two datasets together.

p3.3_data <- p3.2_data %>%
  left_join(p3.1_data, by = ".egoID")

The value labels are coded in a manner that will bias how we calculate ego network characteristics.

As you can see, No = 2 while Yes = 1. However, when we calculate the sum, we want to make sure that we only count the Yes’s, thus it makes more sense to code No as 0, and Yes as 1.

Network Components (Fragmentation)
components() identifies clusters of alters who are connected to each other, independent of ego. An ego whose alters split into several components has a fragmented network — the alters don’t all know one another, so ego sits at the center of several disconnected social worlds. An ego with one component has a fully reachable network, at least in terms of connectivity (this doesn’t necessarily mean the network is dense).
We calculate, for each ego: - the number of components, and - the proportion of alters who fall in the largest component (a common fragmentation index — closer to 1 means most alters are reachable from one another; lower values indicate a more splintered network).

data_components <- tibble(
  .egoID = sapply(igraphs, function(g) graph_attr(g, ".egoID")),
  n_components = sapply(igraphs, function(g) components(g)$no),
  largest_component_size = sapply(igraphs, function(g) max(components(g)$csize)),
  prop_largest_component = sapply(igraphs, function(g)
    max(components(g)$csize) / vcount(g))
)

Network Centrality
Centrality measures describe positions of individual alters within an ego’s network, rather than the network as a whole. To turn them into ego-level variables, we take two approaches: (1) summarize the alter-level scores (mean, max) across each ego’s alters, and (2) use igraph’s centralization functions, which collapse alter-level centrality into a single Freeman-style graph index — how dominated the network is by one or a few central alters (0 = evenly distributed, 1 = a pure hub/star structure).
Betweenness identifies “broker” alters — those who sit on the shortest path between two other alters. A network with high betweenness centralization is one where a single alter (or few) bridges otherwise-separate parts of ego’s social world.
Edge betweenness applies the same logic to ties rather than alters — it flags which alter-alter connections are critical bridges holding the network together (removing them would disconnect otherwise-linked parts of the network).
Closeness captures how quickly each alter can be reached from every other alter on average. High closeness centralization means the network revolves around one or a few well-embedded alters, rather than everyone being roughly equidistant from one another.

data_centrality <- tibble(
  .egoID = sapply(igraphs, function(g) graph_attr(g, ".egoID")),

  # Alter-level betweenness, summarized to the ego level
  mean_betweenness = sapply(igraphs, function(g) mean(betweenness(g), na.rm = TRUE)),
  max_betweenness  = sapply(igraphs, function(g) max(betweenness(g), na.rm = TRUE)),

  # Edge-level betweenness, summarized to the ego level
  mean_edge_betweenness = sapply(igraphs, function(g) mean(edge_betweenness(g), na.rm = TRUE)),

  # Alter-level closeness, summarized to the ego level
  mean_closeness = sapply(igraphs, function(g) mean(closeness(g), na.rm = TRUE)),

  # Graph-level centralization indices (Freeman-style)
  centralization_betweenness = sapply(igraphs, function(g) centr_betw(g)$centralization),
  centralization_closeness   = sapply(igraphs, function(g) centr_clo(g)$centralization)
)
